title: The Three Ripe Pears of the Orchard (TA)
summary: Akbar asks Birbal how to divide three ripe pears among five hungry royal children without cutting them. Birbal resolves the puzzle with familial love.
full_text:
During an afternoon stroll in the imperial orchards of Agra, Emperor Akbar was presented with three magnificent, ripe Chinese golden pears by his head gardener. The fruit was rare, aromatic, and delicious.

At that moment, Akbar's five young grandchildren—three boys and two girls—ran into the garden pavilion, laughing and playing. Seeing the golden pears, all five children crowded around their grandfather, begging for the fruit.

Akbar looked at the three pears, then at the five eager children. Teasingly, he turned to Birbal and said:

'Birbal! Here are three whole pears, and here are five children. I command you: divide these three pears among the five children so that each child is completely satisfied, without cutting, peeling, or slicing a single pear, and without causing tears or jealousy!'

The courtiers shook their heads: 'Three whole pears among five children without cutting? It is mathematically impossible!'

Birbal smiled, knelt down before the laughing children, and asked: 'Tell me, my little princes and princesses: who is the eldest among you?'

A nine-year-old boy stepped forward: 'I am, uncle Birbal!'

Birbal asked: 'And who is the youngest?'

A four-year-old toddler raised her hand with a giggle.

Birbal handed one pear to the eldest boy, one pear to the second brother, and one pear to the third brother.

Now the three boys had pears, and the two little girls had none!

Akbar frowned: 'Birbal! You have left the two girls empty-handed! That is not division; that is unfairness!'

Birbal smiled gently, turned to the three boys, and said:

'Now, noble young princes of the House of Timur: you have heard your royal grandfather preach that a true prince must always protect, cherish, and feed his sisters before himself!

'Will you three brave brothers eat sweet fruit while your little sisters watch with empty hands?'

The three boys looked at their sisters, smiled with genuine family love, and immediately broke the soft, ripe pears in half with their own hands, joyfully sharing the sweet fruit with their sisters and their grandfather!

All five children sat on the marble grass, eating together in blissful unity.

Birbal turned to Akbar with folded hands:

'Sire, mathematics divides with cold knives, leaving fractions and quarrels. But love divides with generous hearts, multiplying joy and teaching children that sharing is the sweetest feast of all.'

Akbar embraced his grandchildren and Birbal, deeply moved by the beautiful moral lesson.
moral: நீதி மற்றும் வாழ்க்கை பாடம்: Wit beats power
